name: Minotaur Labyrinth
geological_features: A planet-spanning canyon network so complex that orbital mapping remains incomplete
Natural stone arches and bridges connecting canyon walls at multiple levels
Mineral deposits that create striped canyon walls in red, gold, and black
specific_features: Navigation equipment malfunctions reported consistently in the deepest canyon sections
Geometric scratch marks on canyon walls at a uniform height of three meters
resources: Iron oxide in concentrated surface deposits
Uranium veins exposed in canyon walls
description: Minotaur Labyrinth earns its name absolutely. The planet's surface is dominated by a canyon network of staggering complexity, a three-dimensional maze of intersecting gorges, overhangs, natural bridges, and dead-end passages that extends across nearly sixty percent of the landmass. The canyons reach depths of twelve kilometers in places, their walls banded in vivid mineral striations that make the whole system look like a wound painted in ceremonial colors.

The thin atmosphere pools in the canyon depths, creating pockets of marginally warmer, denser air that frost crystals drift through like snow. Sound behaves strangely in the narrower passages, reflected and amplified until footsteps echo back as something that sounds like hoofbeats. The sky visible from the canyon floor is a narrow strip of dark blue, and the sense of enclosure is absolute, as though the planet itself is watching from above.

Two anomalies have elevated Minotaur Labyrinth from geological curiosity to active mystery. Navigation instruments malfunction in the deepest sections with a consistency that rules out equipment failure, compasses spinning and altimeters reporting impossible readings. More troubling are the scratch marks found on canyon walls throughout the network, always at precisely three meters height, always in geometric patterns that repeat with variations. No geological process has been proposed that accounts for them.

Expeditions into the deep labyrinth have a poor return rate, not from casualties but from teams emerging at unexpected locations days later than planned, disoriented and unable to account for lost time. The mineral resources in the canyon walls are substantial, but no mining operation has been willing to commit workers to an environment where basic navigation cannot be trusted. The scratch marks continue to appear in newly surveyed sections, always fresh, always at three meters.
